transcript.text: Our Henry has gone a bit weak and sounds rough, sort of rattly growl instead of the normal hum. It's about 12 years old. Bags and filter are new. Worth fixing?

At 12 years old, whether it is worth fixing depends on what is causing that rattly growl. First, please switch off and unplug the vacuum. Detach the hose from the main body and look through it—drop a coin in one end; if it doesn't fall straight out of the other, you have a blockage there. Also check the inlet on the machine itself to ensure nothing is stuck. Once we know that, I will need the model number (usually on a sticker on the body or under the bin) to identify the correct parts and give you a proper repair path.
[Helpful to see: image "Poor suction — what to check first" — Lost suction is usually a full bin, a dirty filter or a blockage in the hose, tube or floor head — check and clear those before suspecting the motor. Switch off and unplug first. Typical layout — your model may differ.]
[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
Thank you. I dropped a coin through the hose and it went straight through, so there's no blockage there. The label on the bottom says HVR 200-22.

Since the airflow path is clear and the filters are new, a 'rattly growl' usually points to mechanical wear inside the motor—most commonly worn bearings or a damaged fan impeller—which is quite common on a 12-year-old machine like your Henry. To confirm this, please switch off and unplug the vacuum. Remove the top casing (usually secured by screws on the base) to expose the motor assembly. Spin the fan blade by hand; if it feels gritty, catches, or doesn't spin freely, the bearings are likely worn. Also, listen carefully while running it: is the noise coming from the motor housing itself? If the motor sounds rough and suction is weak, the repair involves replacing the motor unit. Given the age of the machine, this might be a case where replacement is more cost-effective than repair, but I can guide you through sourcing the part if you wish to proceed.

I have a screwdriver, but I'm not confident taking the motor out. I should also have mentioned that after about five minutes of running there's a hot, burning electrical smell. When I looked at the grille on top in the dim hall, I saw blue-orange sparks flickering inside. Is it safe to carry on using it, or should I stop?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. Stop using it immediately. It is not safe to carry on; the combination of a burning smell, sparks inside the casing, and a rough sound after just five minutes points to a severe internal electrical fault in the motor (likely failing brushes or windings). This presents a genuine fire risk. Please unplug the machine now and do not attempt to use it again until a qualified engineer has inspected it. Given the age of the unit and the severity of these symptoms, replacement is likely the most practical option once you have confirmed there are no other issues.
